title: Houses Are Falling Into the Ocean — And One Rule Makes It Hard to Stop
summary:
Imagine a house that used to be a fun vacation spot. Now it sits 20 feet in the air on wooden stilts, with no stairs and no way in. The ocean comes underneath it at high tide. That's what happened to a house in Rodanthe, North Carolina. Its nickname was Sea 'n Delight. Today, it's falling apart.

The problem is erosion (when the ocean slowly eats away the land). Rising sea levels from climate change make it worse. Since 2020, more than 30 homes have collapsed into the sea in Dare County alone. The National Park Service says over 100 more homes on North Carolina's barrier islands could be in danger in the next 10 years.

So why doesn't someone just tear down the house before it falls? Here's the tricky part: FEMA (the government agency that helps after disasters) gives most flood insurance in the U.S. It pays homeowners after a house collapses — not before. So if an owner tears down a doomed house early, they could lose hundreds of thousands of dollars. "The homeowner is incentivized to wait for collapse and get a payout," says John Ryan-Henry, a policy analyst.

When houses fall, they leave a mess. The Park Service collected more than 480 tons of debris in 18 months. Some washed miles down the coast. Owner Richard Foreman says if he got insurance money, he'd tear his house down tomorrow. A bill to fix the rule is stuck in Congress.
why_it_matters: Beach towns are places families visit on vacation, and the money that helps people rebuild after storms comes from everyone's taxes — so the rules about when to tear down a doomed house affect all of us.

background_read: Rodanthe is a small beach town on the Outer Banks — a long, thin chain of sandy islands along the coast of North Carolina.
The National Park Service (the U.S. government group that takes care of national parks and seashores) looks after this stretch of beach.
In the late 1990s, workers even moved the famous Cape Hatteras Lighthouse (a tall tower that warns ships about the shore) farther away from the sea so the waves would not knock it down.
Article_Structure: WHO: A homeowner in Rodanthe, North Carolina; the National Park Service; FEMA; and policy analyst John Ryan-Henry.
WHAT: Houses are falling into the ocean, but FEMA's flood insurance rule pays owners only after a house collapses — so tearing one down early can cost a family a fortune.
WHERE: Rodanthe, in Dare County on North Carolina's barrier islands, where more than 30 homes have fallen since 2020.
WHY: Rising sea levels from climate change are speeding up erosion, and a bill that would fix the insurance rule is stuck in Congress.

perspectives.description: Owners like Richard Foreman say they would tear down their doomed houses right away if the insurance money came first, instead of waiting for a crash.
FEMA's rule is meant to pay people after a disaster happens, and changing a national insurance program takes time and money in Congress.
When a house falls, tons of debris wash down the shore, so people nearby and the Park Service want the mess stopped before it starts.
